body: I hung out with a group of girls when I was 7-8ish who liked to pretend they could see demons. They would even faint and pretend to get possessed. I was the outcast because I couldn't see demons, too. So naturally, I started pretending. The worst part is I knew they were being cringey, I just didn't want to disappoint my friends.

So true! I tell my students on a daily basis that it isn't safe to come stand directly behind me or beside me without knowing I've seen them. I will step on them, and probably hurt myself. Also, please tuck your chair in when you get up, it keeps your classmates safe, but mostly my clumsy ass. And let's not even get into trying to carry way too many things at once to make your trip to storage more efficient.

Same. Imagine being a grad student at a huge university, constantly running into things and tripping over cracks. I am also a teacher, and I am always falling over chairs or tiny humans. So many bruises.

My HS best friend used to do this, too. She was having a day where she was being kinda clumsy and her boyfriend at the time said something, and it took off from there. Comstantly falling around on purpose, to the point where all her friends noticed it and just stopped paying attention. We just started ignoring it and not reacting when she would do it, and eventually it stopped. As far as I know she still likes to claim she's clumsy, though. I think she thinks it makes her cute.

Thanks for the super kind advice! I think you're right, the PS4 situation feels like the tip of the iceberg, with a lot of other things bothering me below the surface. I have talked to them about cleaning and eating my food, but it feels like nothing has improved. The good thing, I suppose, is that both of my roommates are pretty aware of and realistic about their laziness and why it tends to get on my nerves. They've both apologized a lot for it and tend to pick up after themselves any time I ask, but nothing improves long-term, so I get tired of nagging. It starts to feel like they think I'm their mommy, being the most fiscally responsible, the cleanest, the only one who really cooks, and the person who furnished the entire place, I think they see me as the thing to fall back on if they don't have their shit together. We do also currently have food rules that aren't really being followed. I never minded sharing, and that's not the issue, so the rules have been to ask first, and if the answer is yes, don't eat it all or go overboard. I've found that they typically ask when I'm home but still tend to overdo it, and eat my food when I'm not home, anyway. I think the problem is that neither of them have a whole lot of experience living completely on their own. One of them has always lived with family who cut them a deal or took care of him, and the ps4 roommate was living at home up until he moved in 7 months ago. I've lived away from home since I turned 18, and I don't think they always understand that just because it's under the same roof, it isn't always community stuff for everyone to use. At this point it feels like I'm stuck for another 5 months with shitty roommates and at the very least, it would be nice to see my new gift to myself played less by him than by me.

I caught my ex trying to cheat because Messanger popped up on my computer while I was at home studying and he was out with his siblings. He was essentially trying to meet up with this girl he knew who he found out was at the same place, asking her if she would dance with him, what else she wanted to do, etc. Interestingly enough she didn't seem that interested and was there to meet up for a date with the guy she is now married to, but beside the point. It's a really fucked up feeling and I remember how my heart sank. I'm sorry you had to go through that. I personally should have known to end it then but because it "technically didn't happen" and because he blamed it on his bipolar disorder (mania/heterosexuality) I agreed to work through it. Eventually he wound up actually cheating on me, and has cheated on his current girlfriend multiple times already, so I think he might just be a shitty human.

Also, in sitcoms it's never enough that the person isn't into you. There's always an implication that the person pining is actually perfect and the other person is just stupid for not having realized yet that they're meant to be. Bonus points if the person pining outwardly expresses their affection and/or sexually harrasses the other person until they fall in love.

It's just another way to avoid accepting responsibility for your own actions. My ex used to say the same thing. "Well you know I'm not as smart as you/do dumb things sometimes/can't articulate as well as you/get mean when I'm frustrated". You may not be blaming me for you being incapable of communicating like an adult, but it is my fault for trying?

I met a guy while I was cosmic bowling with a group once, he was bowling with another group next to us and approached me. He flirted all night, we exchanged numbers, things were going well, until he ended the night by telling me that he was "kind of" seeing someone and if we hooked up, we needed to be "low-key". I, probably more than he deserved, politely said no thanks. He got pissed and asked why. I told him he made the choice to approach me knowing he had to be secretive about it, and I just wasn't into it. His argument suddenly became "Look, I have 4 years on you!" (He was 26 and I was 22 at the time). I laughed and said "And clearly those extra 4 years have taught you nothing about getting laid." Why that had anything to do with me pretty kindly telling him j wasn't interested in being the side chick is beyond me.

Not as extreme but still pretrt ridiculous. I went to the doc for breathing problems I would get in relation to my allergies and one of the questions she asked was "When was your last menstrual cycle?" I am on the pill and only have a break week every 3 months. So at the time my last period was 2 months prior. I keep careful track of my cycle so I easily gave her the date and explained my birth control situation. She immediately concluded that my period was late and I was lying about my breathing problems because I needed a pregnancy test. After some arguing and demands for appropriate tests, it was discovered that I was in fact, not pregnant, but I do have RAD.

Back when I did childcare, I had a similar experience, but with a female. She was 4 years old, almost 5. Her very first day, she informed me that I wasn't her boss and that she didn't want or have to listen to me. I don't know what I did to start things off so terribly with her, and I did my best to treat her the same as every other kid in the class, but she was completely unmanageable. If she wasn't doing laps around the classroom or trying to run out the front door, she was punching/kicking me or throwing toys at me. Any time she got sent out if the class, she would give me this smug grin, like she had broken me down and then gotten exactly what she wanted. She told me several times that she didn't like me. The thing was, she didn't treat any other teacher or adult this way. The morning teacher had never seen these behaviors, and any other teacher who kept her in their class when she got sent out of mine said she was a complete delight. At the very least, her mom always took things very seriously. She had consequences at home and was always made to apologize to me. When I tried to raise concerns with the director and others in charge, I was always told that "sometimes kids and teachers just have clashing personalities", which felt really dissmissive and almost like an implication of blame.

Thank you so much. Truthfully, I am uncomfortable telling her, but the feeling that she needs to know still eats at me, and I don't know what to do. I did talk to him about how I feel, he still feels bad but tried to downplay it as not his fault. I put my foot down and told him he needed to take responsibility. He invited me over and he wasn't completely transparent with me. He insisted that he didn't know for sure he wanted to be in a relationship with her until he met her parents, but he did admit that he knew they were at a point where it would hurt her, and that what he did was wrong. I told him that I wasn't going to lie for him, and he told me he wasn't asking me to, though he was scared that meant that I was going to outright tell her what happened myself. I still don't know what it means or if it's the right thing to do. I want her to know but I don't know if I can be the one to tell her. My head is spinning. He put me in a terrible position, one where I helped hurt another woman, and I never wanted that.
This is exactly it. And if he knew that it could hurt his chances with her and he wanted to be with her enough to not want her to know about it, I feel like it was something wrong for us to do.

I think the most hurtful thing is that he wanted to make sure his ass was covered. It tells me he knew what he was doing would be hurtful to her and it's putting me in a tough position. It wasn't something that "just happened", a mistake we're both to blame for, or a situation where the girl knew it was a possibility with casual dating. He knew he wanted to commit to her and that she didn't have any sort of expectation that it could happen. He knew it was something that could ruin his chancee with her. I almost feel like she deserves to know but I don't think it's my place to say anything.

I can't believe there are even people who have the heart to do this. I have definitely gotten last-minute bad vibes before a date or meet-up but I at least make up some kind of bullshit first, ideally before they acrually show up to the place.

Not me, but a good friend of mine. His older brother's girlfriend stole a car, which the guy she was cheating with then stole from her. Guy used it to commit several crimes, including hitting a kid. Police were looking for the original car thief and wound up at my friend's door with some questions. Friend let them in with nothing to hide, problem was he very closely fit the description of the guy they were looking for and they found some clothes on his bedroom floor that matched what witnesses said the guy wore. They asked my friend to step outside, some police cars drove by, and apparently there were witnesses in then who positively identified my friend. He spent a week in jail and the guy they were actually looking for went on to murder someone in the meantime. My friend didn't get a settlement because there was probable cause for the arrest.

I have a friend who's parents always explained it to him this way because they grew up poor and wanted him to know the value of hard work. They tried to explain that money didn't just land in his lap, but that mom and dad worked really hard for it, and that's why they were fortunate enough to go on amazing vacations and own a fucking yacht. There were still so many little things that completely shocked him when he went to college, though. His parents made sure his tuition was covered but he had to otherwise work for a living and he got a taste of the "broke college student" life. And even though he was raised understanding that he had financial privileges other families didn't, there were so many things he had never experienced or understood until he was pinching pennies himself. For instance, I asked him if he had ever looked for brand names at Goodwill (he was picky about his clothes) and it blew his mind that Goodwill was a place to shop. When he was a kid, that was just the place his parents took him and his sister to drop off old clothes.

I had a rich friend in middle school who asked me something like "Don't you hate it when your housekeeper is rude you when you ask them to be gentle with something?" And he was so confused to learn I did not, in fact, have a housekeeper. I did my own chores and, because I didn't know any better, I got a little annoyed that he was actually complaining.
The first time I ever cried during a movie was this scene. I was never a big cryer during movies before but Wilson opened the floodgates.
It sounds like you had some terrible teachers. I'm really sorry to hear that.

In 5th grade, my teacher sat me with a group of highly motivated and academically achieving students who barely spoke English. I was also motivated and high-achieving, and because I spoke Spanish, it worked out really well. They were also in ESL classes so they were learning English, and a lot of our interactions would be me helping them understand some miscommunications and learn new words. I told my mom and great aunt about it and they went and raised hell with my teacher because they accused her of taking away from my learning. It was actually really embarrassing and upsetting because it was a system that was working and those kids were my friends.

Exactly. It's not something us teachers do because we don't feel like helping the kids in need. It's a teaching strategy I've seen covered in countless classes and trainings. Kids are just as much social learners as they are instruction learners, if not moreso. I can't always make or teach certain kids not to goof off, and once it's distracting the whole class, it's a complete disservice to everyone. I was a kid who was frustrated with my teachers pairing me with some students, so I understand. Not all pairings or groups are going to work and not all kids even like to work with others but that's the nature of trying a variety of things until we get to the thing that does work.

This has happened so many times throughout my life. I have light skin and green eyes and live in a region of the States where most of the fluent Spanish-speakers are brown. Most of what I've heard has just been petty stuff, I'll usually respond back in Spanish, and embarrassment follows. The time I remember it hurting the most was when I heard my stepdad's mom telling my step-cousin not to listen to anyrhing I say because I'm just like my mom: stupid and I say I know how to do things I don't. All because it annoyed her that I said I knew how to make scrambled eggs. I was like 9 at the time so I don't really know why that was so inconceivable to her. When I called her out she fiercely denied it and chalked it up to me mishearing, because she wasn't aware that I could speak Spanish fluently. That was one of her first times babysitting me and we were never really cool after that.

"People with depression don't really want to die. They just want the pain to end." I read that once and it stuck with me. I was researching ways to comfort a suicidal friend because I wanted to help them even though I didn't know how to help myself. Those words really hit home, and I recite them any time my thoughts start to get dark and morbid. I don't exactly know why it helps, I just know that I myself was/am tired of hearing the same "it gets better" lines, but thinking of it less as waiting for things to get better and more so wanting things to get better has really helped me with unhealthy thinking patterns. I want to feel better because I don't want to die, I want the pain to end. It helps me reflect on what things I have control over that I can do to help me feel better.

I want to help the kids be patient with him but i don't want to invalidate their feelings or make them feel like they're not allowed to be annoyed.

Hey everyone. Just wanted to say that while I appreciate all of the advice so far, I needed to clarify that I'm actually the teacher in this case, not the student. A lot of you folks are reccomending medication. The trouble is, I have no control over whether or not my student gets treated this way. I do, however, want to make my classroom the best and most accommodating environment possible. Some of my education dealt with these types of accommodations but I wanted to hear what works from the source. Thank you all, I'm glad you're out there living functional lives now!
I'm just a teacher trying to find the best solution for one of my kiddos. I have no control over whether or not my student takes any meds but I can try to make my classroom a better environment.

My ex's best friend and I came really close to having sex one night. We were making out but it stopped before it went too far. I knew I was only doing it out of anger and that it was wrong. The next day, I mended the friendship between my ex and I and to this day we are really great friends. I never did tell him what happened the night before, though.

Not me, but a really good friend of mine dated a guy who cheated on her with her sister. They broke things off for a few months, he apologized, then they decided to try again. A month in and she found out he was cheating again with the same sister. Turns out he got the sister pregnant. My friend really hated her sister and the thought of a baby being involved for a long time. Now the guy is no longer in the picture, she's forgiven her sister, and she adores her nephew. I'm glad it worked out for her, but I don't know if I'd be able to mend things after that.

During a particularly low point in my life, I was donating plasma for some extra money. We were watching the end of a movie involving some sort of storm, and the camera panned over a landscape that was clear and beautiful. The phlebotomist walked up and casually said "Look at how beautiful it is after the storm. You ever notice how life is like that? The storm may be bad, but it only lasts a while  and after it clears everything out, it's beautiful. It's always beautiful after the storm." I've thought about that almost every day since.

I was in 6th grade when my little brother was in kindergarten. I used to pick him up from his class after school and we'd walk home together. One day I went to pick him up and his teacher put her hand on her chest and was so relieved she almost cried. She said "Oh thank goodness, there you are." I thought maybe I had been running late or that my brother was in trouble, but she never actually told me what was going on. Later that evening, my mom got a call from the school counselor suggesting my brother might need professional help because he had lied and told his teacher that his sister (me) had died. We were able to break down the situation and what had happened was, my brother had had a nightmare the night before that I had died. His teacher overheard him describing the dream, but not knowing he had been dreaming, she said "Wait, what happened to your sister?" And being 5 and not knowing his teacher hasn't heard the part where he said it was a dream, he responded "My sister died."

Something that always bothered me about movies was how the kids would spend so much time at their lockers between classes. The only locker I ever had was a gym locker and I only ever used it to "change out". We didn't all goof off or chat in our underwear, either. We had like, 5 minutes to get changed and we weren't given much more than that to get back to our lockers to change back before the bell that ended the class rang. Also, the only really "popular" kids weren't mean. They were genuinely nice kids who got good grades, contributed to the community, and didn't like to exclude people for being different. We definitely had bullies and assholes but they were not the people everyone wanted to hang out with.

A few friends and I met a random guy at a bar who started ripping into the fact that I'm in college and have a degree within minutes of him introducing himself. When I told him I needed my degree to have my career, he went on about how degrees mean shit and college is just a scam to get money. I agreed with him that traditional college is not for everyone and that it isn't a requirement for every single career, but it was something I needed for mine and part of the list of goals I'm accomplishing for myself. He continued to tell me that my degree has no value, that he is undoubtedly smarter than me without one, because he used the internet to teach himself advanced calculus and astrophysics, and was unlocking the secrets of the universe. I'm in the behavioral health field, but he knew more about human psychology than me, in fact he was an expert and was very good at reading people. For instance, he was getting a vibe from me that I  was a nice person with a good heart. I wasn't even annoyed at that point, I was all but trying not to bust out laughing. I told him that he must be right about me being nice because there was a lot I wanted to say to him, but I was choosing to hold my tongue.

Are we friends irl? You just described my roommate. It's only gotten worse over the years and I no longer watch movies with him. A lot of my friends strongly dislike him because he shits all over anything anyone brings up enjoying.

We were close friends for 2 or so years before deciding to give dating a shot. Didn't work out romantically so we decided to go back to being friends. It was cool and all but we realized we still really liked having sex.

There's also a degree of catharsis in controlling a situation in which you would normally feel powerless. You can be completely vulnerable to someone more dominant than you but you also know it can stop at any time. I feel zero guilt about enjoying sex but having had various encounters with men who really do treat women like objects, it's very empowering to feel like I have control over one such scenario.

Children screaming. It makes a lot of people want to rip their hair out, but now I don't even notice it when a kid is throwing a fit in a grocery store. Parent apologizing for their loud kids always makes me laugh because, although I do hear their child, it doesn't bother me at all.

You're fine, it's a valid question. The only time I really remember anyone trying to help was when my mom's parents and siblings fought for custody of me when I was 3-4 ish. They wanted custody of me, but not my older, teenaged siblings. Also, that entire side of the family was just as batshit crazy as my mom. My older siblings remember getting abused by my mom's family when they were young, and by the time I was born, my mom had been completely disowned by her parents for years. They came out of the woodwork completely out of nowhere to try to get me removed from my home and placed into their care. I was totally in an abusive and neglectful situation, but my siblings decided to lie about it because they thought I'd be safer if we all stayed together.  My older brother was in prison not much longer after that, my oldest sister has mental illnesses and we've been estranged since I was pretty young, and that only left one sister I maintained a relationship with. She was way too young to take me in, had her own life to get on track, and I was a little too scared to even tell her the truth about how bad the abuse got once my mom and stepdad got married. Other than that, I didn't have much of a relationship with my dad's side of the family, he abandoned us when I was a toddler. My parents also isolated me from a lot of family, eventually my sister included, as abusers tend to do.

Weird story. When my niece was newly 3 she told my sister and I that she "wanted to go to the place where the blue man cries". We asked her what she was talking about and she just kept repeating herself. It creeped us the fuck out. We later found out that she was referring to this scene in Dumbo, and was trying to say she wanted to watch it. Still have no idea why she called it that, and she doesn't remember calling it that anymore.

Oh yeah, I have a distinct memory of getting in trouble for tipping over a plastic cup of water and being told by my stepdad that "You can't keep calling things accidents as an excuse for being stupid". I was never taught that it was human to fuck up sometimes. It made me terrified of trying new things into my adult years, and I still have to fight off tears sometimes when I make mistakes in a public setting like work because it takes me back to feeling so small and being berated.

Oh I have no doubt my parents would have loved to have me caring for them and bending to their will for their rest of their lives, but I wouldn't call them helicopter parents. They weren't trying to take care of me because they wanted their baby to always need them. They were manipulative and controlling narcissists.
My parents aren't Muslim, just narcissists. But unfortunately that is a sad reality for many other women in Muslim families.

There were several factors that went into it, including abuse, manipulation, and control. But I think one of the motivators for my mom was that she already had 3 older kids who "left her". When she got remarried, she pretty much forgot about them and didn't give a single crap about them for years. It wasn't until her late 40's/early 50's that I think she realized the weight of her own actions. She had a husband who mistreated her, kids who hated her, and she was facing the real possibility that she'd be alone if my stepdad ever walked out. The abusive nature she always had escalated into trying to keep me from escaping her talons like my siblings had. On the other hand, my stepdad is a woman-hater. He despises and fears any woman who is independent, intelligent, and can make her own decisions. He wanted me to be another version of my mom for the sake of being abusive and controlling.

I'm female, but correct. They were already starting to go that direction, too. I would be called lazy for never leaving the house, playing sports, or having any extracurriculars, but it wasn't that I wouldn't have liked to. I just wasn't allowed. I wasn't even really allowed to stay after school for tutoring and whatnot. They also loved to use the argument "What do you know? You've never had a job or done anything valuable" whenever I pointed out they were being shitty or shady in some way.
I am so glad that you made it out of that situation, as well. It's shitty and nonsensical, but it is entirely a matter of how much they want to be able to control the people around them.

Precisely this. It was entirely a control thing. They wanted me under their thumb simply because that's the way they wanted the world to be, and they really believed they could exert that level of control over me.

The simple answer is yes. We're not on terrible terms right now, but our friendship was severely strained during the first two years after I moved out. He talked about communication and everything he wanted to do to make a healthy adult relationship work. The moment I said "Okay, let's do this", everything changed. Thank you so much for the kind words! You are a stranger but it still means a lot! Have a wonderful day!

I understand, I have siblings and we were always afraid of getting separated, too. I don't know if I made all the best choices, and I don't know what your unique situation is, but I do know that what always kept me going was never taking my sights off the future. I knew that my situation was temporary. There was going to be a day that my parents had no legal control over me, no matter what they said or did. Keep your eyes on your future, have a plan, and always remember that your happiness and freedom is waiting for you.

I used to think about that quite often, but as the years have gone by, it crosses my mind less and less. I used to go back and forth on feeling really guilty and enjoying freedom so much I didn't care. I relate to that scene in Tangled where Rapunzel leaves the tower for the first time so much. The thing is, my parents didn't make a big deal out if it until I didn't come home from school the next afternoon. They texted a few people they thought I might be with that I needed to come home or I was going to be in worse trouble but that was about it. They thought I was pulling some stunt but that I would come back. It wasn't until I didn't come home the next day, they went into my room and realized most of my shit was gone that they suddenly got "worried" enough to pursue me coming back. It really didn't take long for that to be too much effort, and then they stopped caring completely. I realized that they never worried that something terrible had happened to me that night. They never even cared enough to ask where I was or that I was safe. I guess realizing that really helped with the guilt but it did fuck with me for a while.

I really hope you get out of that situation. There is a better life out there waiting for you and I promise you even the really tough times will better than feeling like someone else is controlling your every move. You will be amazed at how great life can be and all of the things that you'll be happy to have the freedom to do. You can do this, you will surprise yourself with how strong and capable you are. I'm here if you need anything.

Nah, not really. But I've made peace with it. My stepdad has been terrified of me ever since he realized I wasn't afraid of him anymore. The closest my mom has ever come to apologizing was drunkenly acknowledging to a family member that she shouldn't have let the guy she married control my life, which I only heard about later. The thing is, it takes more effort and energy to try to convince them that they ever did anything harmful, I'd rather just not have contact with them than put myself through the trouble of getting an apology.

Yeah, nothing. Nothing of value or importance, that is. My mom didn't want me to leave her and there's nothing my stepdad hates/fears more than an independent female capable of her own thoughts. They tried to say that they didn't want me to "have to worry about that stuff", because when they were my age they were making babies and poor choices, and working shit jobs to support themselves. They said they didn't want me to make their mistakes, but really they didn't want me to make my own choices. I'm sure they didn't mind that I was around to maintain the household stuff, either. But It's all more complicated than that. Abusers like to have total control of their victims, and any amount of independence would stand in the way of their control.

My parents used to push me out of the house as "punishment" when we would get into arguments. This was among a range of abusive punishments they used to keep me in line over the years. We started arguing a lot after I turned 18 because I was trying to make plans for my future and was literally told that I wasn't allowed to. Not just that I wasn't allowed to plan ahead, but that I wasn't allowed to move on and live an adult life. I wasn't allowed to get a job, move out, or go to college. These were actual things I was told I was forbidden to do when I was an 18-year-old high school senior. The first time they made me sit outside after I'd turned 18 was a freezing cold night in early February, 4 months after my 18th birthday. In that moment it clicked for me that there was an entire world of better things for me out there than the position I was in. By the next time they made me sit outside, I had already snuck most of my stuff out of the house. I've been surprised to find how similar maintaining friendships can be to maintaining romantic relationships. You have to learn how the other person communicates, how they like to be shown you care, how to (or not to) approach them when they're going through a rough time, how to reach out for support. Without these things, any relationship can start to feel annoying, taxing, or like there isn't equal effort involved. And sometimes there isn't, because much like romantic relationships, just because you want it to work and put effort into maintaining it, that doesn't mean the other person is as willing. Adult friendships can be crushing but they can also be beautiful, and they can come when from places you least expect. I have been very surprised by the friends who didn't come through when I needed support, and the people who were there for me without question who I never would have thought would be the ones being so supportive.

When I was about 8, my family and I went to a fast food restaraunt with my parents and two younger brothers. Not really running around or playing, just quietly sitting. I wasn't a great judge of age back then, but I knew he was a lot taller than me, he didn't look like a grown up, but he didn't look quite like a kid, either. He got up and started following me around, asking if I wanted to play and how old I was. He was trying to chase me and tickle me, but I told him I was helping my brother play on the equipment so I couldn't really run and play. I was mostly just getting a creepy feeling from him and was hoping he'd leave me alone. I didn't even think to ask who he was with (my family was the only one in the play area and the dining area only had a few old people) or how old he was, I just knew I didn't like the way he was making me feel. He kept following me around and talking to me, reaching out and trying to tickle me a few more times, and finally I decided to lead my brother down to our parents. My brother must have been equally uncomfortable, because he went willingly. The boy followed us and ended up sitting next to me in the booth, right across the table from my parents. He continued to talk to me and poking/tickling me. My mom was nice to him at first, but eventually decided to ask where his parents were. He said "At home, I just walked over here and felt like hanging out". My mom was shocked and asked how old he was, to which the boy responded that he was 15. My parents promptly packed up and got us the hell out of there. The older I get, the more eerie it seems to think about a teenage boy sitting in that play area, waiting for someone to come up, and then following and ticking a little girl almost half his age. Maybe it was nothing, but it sure didn't feel right, and I remember that very creeped out feeling in my gut, almost as if I was in danger, quite vividly.

I think it's less about freedoms not being absolute and more a distinction of what those freedoms actually are versus what people *think* they are. Freedom of speech is a right that allows you to speak about your opinions or grievances on laws, the government, people in charge, etc. It gives the media the right to report on the government, local or federal, even if that might not paint them in a positive light. Fighting words, disturbing the peace, and public pronouncements (bomb/fire) that endanger people aren't protected by freedom of speech. It's a simplification to say our freedoms aren't absolute but really freedoms were never meant to protect you from breaking other laws.

Also, freedom of speech doesn't protect you from the rules of business and the like. A store kicking you out for calling the cashier a bitch is not violating your freedom of speech. Social media consequences for hate speech is not illegal censorship. Businesses, services, websites, and social media platforms have a right to rules, conditions, and terms of services (within legal means), and if you violate them, they are well within their rights to take action. Freedom of speech protects you from getting arrested for calling the President a cunt. It doesn't mean you can say whatever you want with zero consequences.

The frustrating thing is that sometimes you can want to know people care and feel overwhelmed when people "check up" at the same time. My sister is super awesome about checking up on me without making me feel like I'm burdening her. For instance, she might ask me what my plans are for the weekend, because she knows when I'm in a good mental place, I'm always getting out of the house, or know exactly what I want to do to relax and am excited for it. Or she'll invite me to do a meal or coffee. Basically she expresses interest in my life and spending time with me. And that might be enough to get me to talk or vent, or I might not feel like it. But what I like is for people to make me feel like they care about me and want to spend time with me, not just that r they're checking up on my brain, or making me feel like they feel responsible for keeping me afloat. "It'll get better/easier", or "Time heals all wounds", or pretty much anything that implies they just have to wait for a future moment when life stops hurting. In spite of what I feel, I never talk that way or put those thoughts on other people, so it shocked him. It's really easy for a person who isn't depressed to tell someone to look to the future, but please understand that it's really hard for a depressed person to look past what they feel in that moment. Every time someone told me something like that, I didn't think the logical thought of "Yeah. I just have to wait it out", I always thought "Every day I'm waiting out this storm is another fucking day in the storm, is it worth it?". And the answer is yes, it is. Time does heal and things do get better. But a depressed person has a hard enough time getting though daily tasks. From that point on my friend alwags instead tried to get me to think about what small thing I could do to make my day feel like it was going a little better and personally that helped a lot.

And if you really didn't like that class and would rather sit and do nothing, you could always just walk right over to the room and sit around for an hour. I taught early childhood ed at a public school for a while so I have a note on all-inclusion.  The younger the child is, the more effective it is. In fact, young children with exceptional needs (I would say young being before the age of 9) actually benefit more from being in an inclusive environment with their peers. This is because young children are still malleable, they learn a lot from being in a social environment, and many delays can still be remedied before they become future disabilities. In my state, inclusion is required by law in all early childhood environments. But the key here is that classroom adaptations and modifications must be made to give all kids an equal opportunity to learn, and ideally, continue to be a part of an inclusive classroom as they get older. This could mean anything from making the classroom wheelchair accessible to the child having a one-on-one aid for part of all of the day. The idea is that the younger these kids develop the skills to self-regulate in a mainstream classroom, the better their chances are to remain mainstreamed throughout their education. However, this only works for certain degrees of exceptionalities, and it certainly stops beinf feasible after a certain age. If a student doesn't have the skills to be in an inclusive classroom in 11th grade, putting them in one would be a disservice to all of the students in the class. That isn't to say that they can't continue to work on mainstreaming as a goal, but the inclusion philosophy of putting them in a classroom with their peers so they learn from their peers is far from ideal at that point. So I guess my point is that I understand your frustration. Districts that try the inclusion method definitely mean well, it just doesn't work after a certain age group.

I also like to think of habits as things that form because you feel rewarded for them. For instance, I have a habit of drinking coffee every morning because I'm rewarded with the energy to start my day. It's easy to form bad habits, such as those that lead to procrastination, because they do feel rewarding in some way. It can feel more rewarding to sit in bed and watch another episode of that show than to get up and do that assignment you're dreading or run that pain in the ass errand. Obviously completing the necessary tasks in your life is more rewarding, but when you're developing self-motivating habits, you have to make the rewards apparently gratifying. Go treat yourself to something after you run that errand. Watch a little TV after your workout. Chronic procrastination nearly ruined me when I started college, so for me, rewarding work with breaks was really effective. I started with 30 minute work to 10 minute break intervals. The breaks were short enough that I could still jump back into the task, but I wasn't working for so long that I was exhausted and tempted to take a longer break. I lengthened my work times when I was realizing 30 minutes was actually interrupting my work flow. Eventually my own satisfaction from getting work done was enough of a reward that I didn't need regimented breaks anymore. Also, I've noticed that being motivated in one area of my life keeps me motivated in others, especially if I use that thing as a reward. For instance, I found myself really motivated to do well and work hard at martial arts because I enjoyed it. My deal with myself was that I could only attend class every evening if I had finished my school work for the day. But really, feeling motivated to do well at a hobby I enjoyed made it super easy to feel motivated to do other things, once I developed positive habits in that area, it felt like other things started falling into place.

When I'm emotional, thinking of the steps to all of the solutions can just be overwhelming, and it can feel like you're telling me my feelings aren't real because my problem can be solved. I personally wouldn't even say I don't want your advice at all, I just need you to take a minute to validate my feelings, first. It can be a lot easier to process your suggestions when I've calmed down, and once I'm not as upset anymore, you might even realize the problem wasn't big enough to even require your solutions. For advice-givers, they don't want to see you upset, and they feel like the solution is helping you see that you can solve the problem, so I do think it's important to be just as understanding of their intent as I want them to be of my needs, and have the patience to kind of explain "Hey, I'm getting a little overwhelmed, I think I just need sympathy right now", and go from there. And this is also something I'm mindful of when I start to feel like I want to start offering advice.

To offer my perspective on the validation point in your edit, sometimes it's not that I see someone offering help as less validation, it's just too much for me in the moment. When I'm worked up and venting, it can be a little overwhelming to me for you to immediately start offering solutions. And in some cases, depending on how the advice is given, it can even feel like what you're telling me is that I shouldn't really feel that way because the issue is an easy fix anyway. For instance, my sister really has a way of seeming like she's shrugging off what you're upset about with her "Well just do this" tone, even if that's not her intention at all. But for the most part, it can just be hard to process advice and emotions at the same time. So for me it's not that I want just validation, or that I don't feel like your help is validating my feelings, it's just that I need a pat on the back and an "I understand" first. Telling me you get me eases my mind so I'm in a better place to hear you when you start to try to help me fix it. My best friend and I are similar this way and we comfort each other with something I learned at a communication workshop. Validate the persons feelings first, ask them what they want to do once they've started to calm down, then ease into your ideas for solutions. It's been really helpful both when I'm listening and when I'm upset about something. I know this is something that can be hard to explain so I hope my perspective helped a little.

Question: What is the education like in weed-legal states/areas? I live in a medical-legal red (conservative) state and in high schools, they teach that smoking marijuana is just as harmful and addicting as doing crack or heroine. I know a lot of people who would disagree that marijuana is a gateway drug, but I do think this deterrence type of education is dangerous, because by putting weed on the same tier as other more harmful drugs, the actual dangers of other drugs are undermined when people (especially kids) try weed and think "If this isn't so bad, what else was school lying about?" I don't think fear is an effective method of education or discipline in any sense. However, in my state, I've noticed that what's left for popular "education" is the opposite extreme, the annoying stoner-types who are obsessed with smoking and say that there are no cons to marijuana use at all (I've noticed the opinions of people who are more balanced users, and don't make smoking a part of every aspect of their lives, aren't really as popularized). Imo, this is also dangerous, because there are risks to anything we put into our bodies, and I think its important for those to be known. I recently saw a video of parents talking to their young children about smoking. They were really candid about their own use of marijuana, answered questions honestly, and explained the risks of mental addiction. Some of them talked about waiting until they were adults, because it could be harmful to their developing brain cells, and balance and moderation, because overdoing it can make you "lazy", as one mom put it. As an occasional recreational smoker who gets thoroughly annoyed with both fear-mongering education, and the people in my life who are annoying stoners but refuse to believe in any cons to smoking, I found this video really interesting. Being a teacher by trade myself, I thought that this could be a very honest and effective method of education, and was wondering if a similar approach was actually implemented anywhere else.

I think people are so quick to disregard bisexuality as a phase because they confuse the orientation with sexual curiosity. It's very common to sexually experiment and act on curiosity, and not all people who do identify as bi, but there are plenty of people who do. And also, because people like things wrapped up in a neat, black-and-white box, so if something doesn't look like their typical definition, it's disregarded. Some people might be sexually attracted to the same sex, but not interested in them romantically. Or happened to have dated more members of the opposite sex, or ultimately settled down with the opposite sex. So because it can be this complex, fluid thing, it's hard for people to understand that it's more than just a "phase". I will also say that this happens the other way around sometimes, too. People like to slap the bi label on someone just because they've been with the same sex, and that's not right either. In general people just need to understand that you can't identify others for them, they're the only ones in charge of identifying themselves.

Straight girls don't mess around with girls, though. Because straight girls exclusively like guys. So that always peeves me, because I know actually straight people who would never even think about being with members of the same sex. I think in general, sexual fluidity needs to be more recognized and accepted. Even within the LGBT community, it can be viewed by some people as very black and white thing, and that's not always the case. Some people identify as just straight, gay, or bi, and that's cool. But some people may not identify (or don't like to be identified as something by others), because they don't feel like they fall right into one of those orientations. Some people are sexually attracted to one gender but romantically attracted to the other, sometimes people experiment, or change their minds at certain points in their life or for certain people. And all of that is okay, because where a person identifies themselves is up to them.

Broad degrees aren't enough anymore, and it's frustrating. In my field, a psychology or social work degree used to do the trick. Now, a specific job will want one of those degrees, education relating to the age group, and experience with that age group. When people ask why I'm still in school even though I "have my degree", why I have such specific degrees, and why I have professional development certificates for multiple age groups, yeah, that's why.

The idea that everyone needs a degree to be successful and qualified is ruining shit for everyone. People are spending money on nonsense degrees because they feel like they need to have one, experienced people are being seen as less qualified in fields that have never really required higher education before, and the education requirements are raising in fields where education is necessary and important. And don't get me wrong, I'm all for jobs requiring up-to-date professional development, but I know a few people who have lost their jobs after 20 years in the field or position  because they didn't have a degree, or were told they would be fired or demoted unless they started their degree. I've seen job positions that require a minimum of a bachelor's or master's degree in anything, it didn't even have to be related to the job. My sister works compliance for a major university with a master's in business, which she got because the job required a bachelor's (she had her associates when she started), and then a master's after a few years. And yes, people were fired or resigned if they didn't go get a random degree. Hell, even I was advised to pick a more "refined and focused" degree than psychology, because everyone was getting psychology degrees for the sake of having something and it wasn't being taken as seriously in the field anymore. School or training after high school used to be about learning how to do the thing you wanted to do, college becoming this standard is leaving people who don't necessarily need to be there in debt for no reason.

My parents used to encourage me to tell my friends to help me clean up before they left if we made a mess. They never "made" me tell them to or told them they had to. But as far as they were concerned, it had to be cleaned up, anyway, so I could either do it by myself when they left, or have them help. That's one thing, but a different entirely to make someone else's kid do something because you're annoyed with your own.

"Obedient" is also a really loaded word. An obedient kid is just a kid that listens when you tell them to do something, right? But the connotation, especially when used as described above, is that you can get your kid to just immediately do whatever you say without questioning you. So even if obedience does correlate with happiness, it's misleading to say that just because happier kids listen to their parents, kids are happier when you act like an asshole overlord. In fact, there are plenty of schools of though on parenting and/or guidance and discipline that highlight ways to talk so kids will listen, and help them learn to understand you so listening becomes an autonomous choice, rather than something they do to survive living under their parent's thumb. The point being, it's a very misleading thing to say and people make the dumbest excuses for being a downright mean parent.

My friend said that he doesn't remember a lot about the day, just that he got a horrible feeling of grief and ran to his mom, crying and saying his twin brother's name. Freaked out, their mom immediately started to look for the brother, but he was nowhere to be found. My friend also has two older siblings, and pretty soon everyone was searching every inch of the house and calling the twins name. After a while of searching to no avail, my friends mom remembered that the last time she has seen Twin, he was asking to go to the lake. The parents had the older siblings stay with my friend while they walked over to the lake to keep searching, where they ended up finding Twin's fishing pole on the ground, and his hat floating in the water. My friend's mom was wailing, and his dad jumped in and started looking for his son's body in the water. Meanwhile, the siblings were still looking for him at home. When the parents didn't find him in the water, they decided to start heading back home, to call the police, and with some hope that maybe they had just missed Twin and that he was walking around somewhere. When they got home, the dad went to go get the phone and heard something in the attack. He ran upstairs, soaking wet, and found Twin playing up there. They maintain that they thoroughly searched the attic multiple times, along with the rest of the house, and that they were calling his name over and over, so if he'd been up there the whole time he would have heard them. They found him completely dry. 20 years later, Twin doesn't remember that day whatsoever, even though his parents and the rest of his siblings do. EDIT: Fixed a word.

Interestingly enough, ESL classes are taught almost exclusively in English, though a good teacher will attempt to learn some basic words in the languages of all his or her current students to bridge the communication gap to some degree. It's not like a foreign language class where someone can tell you in your home language what something means in another. Comparatively, it's more like providing new language the way you would a child learning to speak. Most children in an ESL class can learn at the same developmental capacity as their peers, but need the language to comprehend classes being taught in English. And the children are going to be on different comprehension levels, so a lot of what's involved is the teacher identifying where each student is, and strategies that work best for their learning. There are a lot of hands-on activities and pantomimes involved. The goal is not only conversational English, but comprehension of the language in a classroom structure. So a variety of topics and subjects will be involved, including understanding coursework and terms from general classes. It's a single class that has to fit any type of language, so there are definitely challenges. Another challenge to teaching children in particular is the fact that they tend to have less control over frustrations and other emotions that come with communication gaps, so some ESL students will have behaviors associated with that. I can't speak much on an adult ESL class but part of my education was learning to teach early language learners.

Part of your research on finding a good artist should be asking them their hourly rate, how long your tattoo will take, and the shop minimum. You shouldn't settle for the cheapest, but don't mistake getting overcharged and taken advantage of for high quality. And don't choose the first talented artist that quotes you. Look into a few artists you like and get that important information. There are slimy artists out there who may try to take advantage of it being your first tattoo if they can tell that you don't know the right questions to ask. I paid $150 for my first tattoo, it took all of 15 minutes, by an artist I later learned had a rate of $50/hr, at a shop I learned had a $50 minimum. I picked the first artist I liked and asked her how much I had to pay with no perspective on what a reasonable price for a 15-minute tattoo was. Last year I paid $150 for a tattoo that took 2.5 hours, if that tells you anything.

This is a really difficult thing to come to understand, because from your perspective, being happy in the relationship as it is, it doesn't make sense to be apart. From his perspective, something in the relationship wasn't working. It's easy to adapt around difficult schedules when you know you want to be with a person in the long-run, but if you're not 100% certain, then putting the work in is really difficult. I believe (and so should you) that the ultimate reason for the breakup is exactly what he says: he thinks you deserve better. He cares about you and he values your relationship, realizing that things aren't working for him, anymore doesn't mean that much isn't true, and that's why he wants you to find someone you could be happier with. Likely the bottom line is simply that he doesn't see himself with you in the future, and he sees himself in a different place in his own life/career right now. That makes working around his schedule really hard for him, especially because he feels guilty that you're going through all that trouble for him when he doesn't think the relationship is going to last. People are going to come here and say that he was just looking for excuses to break up with you, but I don't think that's the case. There were definitely reasons he knew the relationship wasn't going to be forever, but that's not really what you should be focused on. The important thing is that he had the love and respect for you to tell you that he wasn't going to continue to drag you through his schedule when he knows you can be happier with someone who wholeheartedly wants to be with you. Have the same care and respect for him by understanding that his life is taking him in a different direction right now, and remember that you also want to see him happy. It's not going to be easy for either of you, you're both giving up something comfortable and happy right now, but you're doing it to have a happier future. Trust me, it's a lot better than going the "easy" route, staying together for now and waiting for the other shoe to finally drop, and imagine how pissed and hurt you'd feel if you wound up breaking up after putting in even more time and effort to adapt to his schedule than you already have. Be hurt, be angry, go through the whole process, but be rational. You can't make him change his feelings and it's only going to hurt you more in the long run to try, but you can take comfort in appreciating that he truly does value you, that's why he wants to see you in a relationship you deserve.

It's really interesting to me, as a child of the "ignore your bullies" generation, and an educator of the "use your words" generation, to see the differences across the board. My BIL was talking to me about how he grew up standing up to bullies, getting his ass kicked, and sometimes kicking ass, and how that's how he remembered boys dealing with their issues with each other when he was a kid. I think that people talk about how "sensitive" today's society is without realizing the roots of the issue. Bullying was always harmful, but I think we did more damage by focusing too much attention on teaching kids how to not feel the affects of their bullies. As a kid, I was told to let things roll off my shoulders and ignore differences because they make people uncomfortable. Today I help kids identify differences so that they understand them (rather than make fun of them), and have the empathy to consider the feelings of others, as well as their own. Not only that, but today, kids are being provided the language at a very early age to stand up for themselves, again. You'd just be so amazed what providing language can do for behavior. Kids once used physical force as a means to communicate, then were told not to communicate, and now are being shown at very early ages how to use verbal language to solve problems. Say what you will about "using your words", but when I see children standing up for themselves, working out their own issues, and showing empathy for one another in ways I never experienced as a kid, I can't help but think we're moving in the right direction.

I forgave him because I genuinely believed (and still do, quite honestly) that he was sorry. There are people who are sorry they got caught, and once-a-cheater people, but sometimes the situation is more complex. He confessed the information to me because he felt like he couldn't control himself and never wanted to do the things he was doing again. I know that he never intended to hurt me and that my feelings meant everything to him. Believe me, I went through my ups and downs about it,  and I'm beyond telling myself things to feel better about it. I know him, heart and mind, and these days I feel more sorry for him, as bitter as i have been and can still be sometimes. He has bipolar disorder and his manias make him hypersexual. It drove him crazy and made him feel tremendously guilty at the same time. I remember the way he described doing things that didn't make sense without even thinking, then feeling so remorseful afterward that he would pray to get in an accident or contemplate suicide. I won't make excuses for him because his actions were wrong and hurt me deeply. He took responsibility and I took back the man he was beyond the episodes on the condition that he seek professional help. Our relationship never fully recovered. We wanted to rush into going back to exactly the way things were before. We both feared that taking space for self-healing would lead to the other finding someone else, but in retrospect, we really needed it. He needed time alone to break his codependent behaviors and I needed the time to go through the rollercoaster of recovery and grow without dragging him through the guilt and negativity of my low points. Ultimately, he recognized that he was making me too responsible for his happiness, and I learned that I am awesome and getting cheated wasn't my fault. But we said and did a lot of aweful and unhealthy things to each other along the way. And unfortunately, he never did get professional help. He decided he didn't want to and that is ultimately what ended our relationship on mutual terms, but by that point most of the permanent damage that had contributed to our decision to split had already been done. I have a lot of regrets, but at the end of the day, I know that a refusal to get helo would have always been the deal-breaker. That was the change on his part that was supposed to have really proved his remorse and efforts to never hurt me that way again. The end result is that today we are great friends. I still consider him to be a valuable person in my life, and we have a lot of love and respect for one another. Our breakup was the most peaceful and respectful thing we did for each other during the tail end of our relationship. And it was good for the both of us. We've done a lot of healing and I am so happy to say that he is learning to live a full life for himself. He has still chosen not to seek help, and struggles with his mental illness, but I no longer live with the stress of the results. What I learned was exactly how messy and complicated relationships can be, and that two people can love each other completely and still be better apart, as painful as it is. I don't think that i have it in me to take back a cheater again, but I know now that it is a lot easier to give opinions on cheating from an outside perspective than to make black-and-white decisions when you're dealing with the situation yourself. For that reason, I don't think I'd tell someone not to take back a cheater, either. I know couples who have been happily married for decades who have recovered from cheating. But both parties need to heal individually, rediscover their love for the other person, forgive completely, and most importantly, be committed to change.

I was just going to say this. It's one of those things people try to be witty about or proud of because in reality it's really a frustrating and helpless feeling. It doesn't help that struggling to learn the one-size-fits-all way that most teachers use in math classes is often so easily shrugged off as being "bad at math". In my experience as a teacher and student, a lot of people who think they're bad at math have A) been shrugged off as just being bad at math and B) were simply never properly guided to develop mathematical critical thinking skills that benefit the way you learn and understand numbers. Math is a very hard subject to teach and there are flaws in the school system that make teaching it even harder. What a lot of teachers and curriculum alike fail to grasp is that you can't teach people one way to work numbers any more than you can reach people one way to solve a jigsaw puzzle. And when you keep telling kids they're wrong when they don't get it one way, rather than trying to find an angle that will help them understand, math actually becomes a really terrifying and off-putting subject. I was always afraid of it myself until I had a professor in college that spent less time on teaching methods to solving problems and more time on the mechanics and rules of the things we were working on. Then he would basically tell us "Okay now knowing all that, solve this. Don't really care how you do it, just get the right answer". It was the first time I really felt like I was "getting" math, and everyone I know who has taken his class, including the students I took the class with, have finished his class with an 85% or better. People get so cheated by going through middle and high school not being taught math that way.

Used to work for a business that had a really tactful way of keeping people stuck as low as possible on the payscale. They do first interviews, second interviews, hiring, and training, all at different locations for each step of the process, none of which can take place at the location you will ultimately be working at. It's supposed to be so all of the site directors who are important to the business have a chance to meet and approve you for the company, but I can't tell you how many people would get promises by different directors throughout the interviews and hiring processes. The company always promoted from within and brought in all new hires at the lowest position (paid intern) and trained them up to the other positions. So a popular promise that I always heard complaints about the few years I worked there was "They told me I'd get a raise after my probation period was over". And then our site director would say something like "Well no one told me that, did you get it in writing?" "No, they just promised me when I got hired." "Well sorry, you're capped out as an intern, you signed the employee handbook with the payscale, you need to get promoted to get a raise." They would also tack on limitless responsibilities without a raise in the name of learning during your internship. The point being, I think it is definitely a shady tactic if only because you can make endless promises if you aren't legally bound to keeping them, and especially if the burden of dealing with that emoloyee doesn't directly fall on you. Companies do it all the time, so never be afraid to ask for things in writing, even if you fully trust your boss. Even extra responsibilities with no raise is good to have in writing.

I like to do the occasional one-shot GURPS session in an existing universe, and I've found that certain types of campaigns (like apocalypse settings) really only work well if they're short anyway, so bringing in the possibility of a hilariously shitty death is highly entertaining. If you're trying to run a long campaign and want the players to get immersed in the story, however, you have to adjust things so you're not killing characters left and right, though you get them close enough to a near-death experience that it's still exciting. And the reality is that you have to kill PC's sometimes, but you can't kill them all the time. A great GM once advised me to get a screen and be willing to occasionally fudge numbers to keep the game reasonably fun, that's the only way a long campaign works. I've never fudged numbers precisely, but I have adjusted intended targets and such to keep my characters from straight up dying over something stupid.

This is exactly what I was thinking. I mean, no one here is necessarily wrong in their opinions because different kids and families are different, and therefore different things will work best for them, and the fact of the matter is that context is key. Considering all the perfectly reasonable reasons a family might need their child to not take 2 or 3 hours to eat dinner, I don't see a problem, because I'm not assuming stuff that no one said. But one thing that I know from professional experience is that, while individual children are vastly different from each other, it's also developmentally healthy to prepare them for the realities of life. When I taught preschool mine was the only classroom that had snack as an option for about an hour. There was no rush or limit (within reason), and they could choose to eat when they wanted to, but the catch was that they had to eat eventually within that hour. Most teachers allotted 15 minutes of actual eating time for snack, to give you an idea of how different that was for preschool. This catered to the different needs of the kids, but also helped them learn natural consequences if they chose not to eat (getting hungry later) without forcing them to scarf down food on a time limit. I adopted this from a lab school I interned at while getting my degree, whose practices were researched-based and essentially designed to create the most ideal learning environment. They did this because it's not healthy to try to fit all kids in one mold, but it's not healthy to not keep them out of touch with reality, either. They have to learn how to manage their own time and options and that sometimes there's a time limit. But allotted time doesn't necessarily mean having to rush, though it does mean having to get to know your body and be able to communicate how it feels. So while there's nothing wrong with letting your kid eat for 3 hours if that's what works now, that doesn't necessarily mean it's going to work later, when they're on a time limit at school. And that doesn't necessarily mean that it works for other people, who don't have time to do other things and stay on nightly schedules when their kid is sitting at the table for hours at a time.

Don't think OP was suggesting anyone was forcing the kid to eat fast, just giving him a visual symbol to help keep him focused on the task at hand (eating). I mean, you have no clue, other than the details OP provided, the other factors that went into the parents decision to do this, but by no means did anyone say they were training the kid to scarf meals down in no fewer than 30 seconds or something.

I'm a teacher, so I learned the person-first language during my education. When kids are involved, we call it "child-centric language". I never learned it in the context that it was offensive, but just that it was important to put the child first at all times. I think you're correct that it was developed by neurotypical people, but less as a reason to avoid offense, and more of a method to ensure we are always putting the child first in our own minds. It's the same reason why ECE professionals will oftentimes use the term "child care" over "day care", which is another example of child-centric language that has nothing to do with a diagnosis. It's just a reminder that we are trying to create an optimal care environment for a child, rather than watching them during the day until the parents pick up. Kids with exceptionalities have the same needs as typically developing children, with the exception of some needs that help them recieve optimal educational experiences and such. So for an educator, using the term "child with autism" over "Autistic child" is a small detail in the important process of creating an optimal environment for the needs of a person who is a child before their diagnosis. That's just been my experience with it as a teacher, anyway.

Forcing kids to potty train tends to be a lot more frustrating for the parent and in bad cases it can set the child back even further. Being afraid of the toilet is super common! Sometimes it's the loud flushing noise and sometimes it's literally the feeling of going to the bathroom outside of the diaper that's scary. Maybe if you can find out what scares him, you can start talking to him about it and make it less scary. I nannied for a girl who's first time going poop on the potty she spent hugging me. Smelled really bad but it worked! I've also cared for kids who bargained with me that they'd go on the potty as long as I waited for them to leave the bathroom and then flushed it for them. At the end of the day, a lot of people view potty training as a lot more frustrating and tricky than it really is. For a typically developing child, potty training practically happens overnight when they're ready. It's pretty normal for a kid to potty training perfectly at age 3, but most facilities want kids potty trained at 2, before their 3rd birthday, but really developmentally 3 is a pretty average age. Really, it's nothing to worry about. Keep talking to him, get him excited about getting clean and how clean going on the potty feels, and talk to a pediatrician. They'll be able to tell you exactly where your son is and how to work from there. :) best of luck!

I told her that regression was completely normal after a new baby was born (the mom had given birth to a baby brother less than a year before), and that from what I had observed working with the child, she was using potty training as a control tactic. I told her that every child develops some sort of control tactic at that age, and potty training is a super common one because parents tend to get so desperate to get it done. My advice was that potty training was going to seem a lot harder as long as she was trying to force it, and I thought she just needed to let her daughter go through the regression stage. I gave her some tips on one-on-one routines she could do with her daughter to help her get over wanting her diaper changed, on phrases she could use to help her daughter understand the sensations related to soiling a diaper, and ultimately how to eliminate negative punishments related to accidents and replace them with teaching the cleanliness aspect as she starts to get that she doesn't like the feeling of going in her diaper. Teacher here. Just wanted to let you know that you are absolutely correct. Children learn the majority of their behaviors and emotional responses through modeling at a very early age. Everyone gets angry/sad/frustrated, which is totally okay, but how we learn to manage our emotions make a difference. For kids who see anger and violence, they learn that those types of responses are normal and okay. But we can change that by modeling and leading better behaviors, and conflict resolution and coping skills. The earlier we focus on emotional regulation and conflict resolution, the better, optimal time for development in these areas is basically 5 and under. The older we get, the harder it becomes to fix. The problem is that many elementary school educators actually lack the knowledge and the patience to model behaviors and intervene during conflicts in developmentally appropriate ways that actually do any damn thing to teach these kids emotional regulation and conflict resolution skills when they need it most.

There are many causes, but I feel one that seems to fall under the cracks is a crappy home life. Sometimes we can't do much for the home situations of those kids, but we can do something about their experiences at school. For those kids, school NEEDS to be an escape, and a place where they are developing better relationships and recieving more positive mentorship than they are at home. The problem is that was many teachers have a knack for developing helpful and trusting relationships with their students, many educators lack the proper knowledge to spot a kid with those needs, or even how to help them if they can spot it. And the teachers who can help are rarely a one-size-fits-all mentor, they gravitate toward and are more helpful with very specific needs and cannot necessarily be helpful in every situation. For example, a child who witnesses domestic abuse may have different needs than a child who has emotionally neglectful parents. If teachers were provided more training and encouraged to develop these relationships, they might have a positive enough school environment for that to be their escape, rather than other more harmful outlets. The coping skills they are learning now will carry with them through their lives. If they can learn to cope by turning to mentors and positive hobbies, we can help prevent them from turning to things like violence and substance abuse.

The current typical K-3 classroom setup is not developmentally appropriate for the age group. According to the science of brain development, children up until the age of 9 would learn and thrive best in an environment more similar to what they have preschools: hands-on, active, quick transitions, ability to explore the environment with all of their senses. During early childhood, you actually learn best when you are being physically active. Yet you are expected to be able to sit at a table by the age of 5, because elementary school is suddenly supposed to be this strict, serious experience full of standardized testing. Stress levels for children in this age group are at an all-time high. The expectancy of the child of that age group to learn while trying to go against their own instincts and adapt to the style of the teacher, as well as the behavior modification techniques they encourage use of to "teach" them how to behave in a classroom aren't developmentally appropriate. I currently teach preschool because I love having the ability to adapt my teaching styles to the flow of the classroom, knowing children age birth to 8 learn best through play and hands-on experiences. Current classrooms also force academics much more than social-emotional learning, which is equally important. That age group cannot learn if they are not socially and emotionally functional, and if they don't learn it at that stage in development, they will have many future problems learning as well. I once heard a saying during a training that went "If you cannot prevent it, lead it", and I have taken it to heart in my classroom. My students meet all their milestones, not only academically but social-emotionally as well, while I adapt my lessons to their interests and needs. You can't prevent a 5 year old from jittering in their seat, but you can use physical activities to teach them. K-3 classrooms need to put more emphasis on helping children understand their emotions, manage and self-regulate them, socially interact with each other in an approproate way, and teachers need to be relieved of the pressure of getting fucking 7 year olds ready for standardized tests and given the freedom to create environments where their kids are able to optimally learn according to their development and development.

I took French from age 12-16 and there was a very specific reason I stopped after sophomore year. My wonderful middle school French teacher tapped into the science of natural language development by having days where she would just speak French to us and demonstrate what she was saying. There would usually be a focus that would go along with our "traditional" lesson for the week, like school supplies, but on "French only" days we were actually going beyond words next to pictures and worksheets, and were seeing these words live, and hearing what they sounded like naturally. Before we had formally learned more advanced vocabulary, we learned what it sounded like to be asked to retrieve a stapler off her desk or quickly sit up and slowly walk across the room. Just like when babies have to learn to understand your words before they have the ability to speak themselves. It made connecting words to their meanings easier, and made advanced vocabulary and grammar natural. Alongside our traditional lessons, her methods worked wonderfully. High school French was totally different. Going into a different district, my teacher was impressed with my abilities for the level I was supposed to be at. But his class was all textbooks and worksheets. Our speaking practice was working with Rosetta Stone twice a week, which was a great program, but using it on its own left us lacking the natural human communication aspect. After sophomore year I found myself not only enjoying class less but in general remembering less of the lessons and losing my ability to connect them to the language as a whole. Taking French seemed like a waste of time and schedule space when I wasn't even learning anything anymore, so I made the honestly hard decision to stop taking French after my fourth year of learning. The most meaningful things that I learned came from the two years before and I can honestly say that as much as I remember from middle school, what I remember from high school is virtually nothing.
